primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: NSAID-induced reduction in GFR during volume depletion
mechanism: Renal prostaglandins normally support afferent arteriolar dilation, particularly when effective circulating volume is reduced. Cyclooxygenase inhibition lowers prostaglandin synthesis, causing relative afferent vasoconstriction and reduced glomerular capillary pressure.
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with several days of vomiting takes high-dose ibuprofen for osteoarthritis. Two days later, serum creatinine rises despite no urinary obstruction.
lead: Which renal hemodynamic change most directly explains the decline in glomerular filtration rate?
correct: Afferent arteriolar constriction due to reduced prostaglandin synthesis
distractors: Efferent arteriolar dilation due to reduced angiotensin II formation
Afferent arteriolar dilation due to increased prostaglandin E2 synthesis
Efferent arteriolar constriction due to increased angiotensin II formation
Increased glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure from afferent vasodilation
distractor_notes: Efferent dilation is the characteristic direct renal hemodynamic effect of ACE inhibition or ARB therapy, not NSAID cyclooxygenase inhibition.
NSAIDs reduce rather than increase renal prostaglandin synthesis, so afferent vasodilatory support is lost.
Efferent constriction can support GFR during reduced perfusion and does not directly explain NSAID-associated GFR decline.
Increased afferent dilation would tend to preserve or raise glomerular capillary pressure, opposite the observed effect.
key_expl: Prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin help dilate the afferent arteriole. NSAID-mediated cyclooxygenase inhibition reduces these prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole constricts and glomerular capillary pressure and GFR fall, especially in volume-depleted patients.
objective: Explain NSAID-associated acute kidney injury through loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Total-body potassium depletion in diabetic ketoacidosis despite elevated serum potassium
mechanism: Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality shift potassium out of cells, which may raise serum potassium, while osmotic diuresis, vomiting, and secondary renal losses cause a substantial total-body potassium deficit.
vignette: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations, glucose 480 mg/dL, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. His initial serum potassium is 5.4 mEq/L.
lead: Which statement best describes this patient's potassium status before insulin therapy?
correct: Total-body potassium is depleted despite the elevated serum potassium concentration
distractors: Total-body potassium is increased because insulin deficiency prevents urinary potassium loss
Total-body potassium is normal because the serum potassium concentration is elevated
Intracellular potassium is increased because hyperosmolality drives potassium into cells
Renal potassium excretion is absent because ketoacidosis fully suppresses aldosterone secretion
distractor_notes: DKA causes substantial urinary potassium loss through osmotic diuresis; insulin deficiency does not prevent renal potassium depletion.
Serum potassium can be misleading in DKA because transcellular shifts mask a total-body deficit.
Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality favor movement of potassium out of cells, not into them.
Aldosterone is not fully suppressed; volume depletion and renal losses contribute to potassium wasting.
key_expl: DKA commonly presents with normal or high serum potassium because insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality, and acidosis shift potassium extracellularly. At the same time, osmotic diuresis and other losses deplete total-body potassium. Insulin therapy then drives potassium back into cells and can rapidly uncover severe hypokalemia.
objective: Distinguish serum potassium concentration from total-body potassium stores in diabetic ketoacidosis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Parathyroid hormone decreases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption by promoting internalization of apical sodium-phosphate cotransporters, especially NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc, causing phosphaturia.
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism has hypercalcemia and low serum phosphate. Renal function is otherwise normal.
lead: Which tubular change most directly causes the low serum phosphate?
correct: Internalization of sodium-phosphate cotransporters in the proximal tubule
distractors: Increased sodium-phosphate cotransporter expression in the proximal tubule
Activation of the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Increased phosphate reabsorption through ENaC in the collecting duct
Reduced distal tubular calcium reabsorption
distractor_notes: PTH decreases rather than increases proximal tubular NaPi transporter availability.
NKCC2 handles sodium, potassium, and chloride in the thick ascending limb and does not mediate the principal PTH phosphaturic effect.
ENaC transports sodium, not phosphate, in collecting-duct principal cells.
PTH increases distal calcium reabsorption; phosphate wasting is a separate proximal tubular effect.
key_expl: Most filtered phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule through NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc. PTH causes internalization of these cotransporters, decreasing phosphate reabsorption and increasing urinary phosphate excretion.
objective: Explain PTH-induced hypophosphatemia through proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporter internalization.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Beta1 adrenergic receptors on juxtaglomerular cells promote renin release. Selective beta1 blockade decreases renin secretion, reducing downstream angiotensin II and aldosterone activity.
vignette: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and coronary artery disease begins metoprolol therapy. His heart rate decreases, and plasma renin activity also falls.
lead: Blockade of which receptor population most directly explains the decrease in renin release?
distractors: Beta2 receptors on macula densa cells
Alpha1 receptors on glomerular podocytes
Muscarinic M2 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells
Dopamine D2 receptors on proximal tubular epithelial cells
distractor_notes: Beta2 receptors are not the primary adrenergic receptors that drive renin release from juxtaglomerular cells.
Alpha1 receptors on podocytes are not the canonical target controlling renin secretion in this setting.
Metoprolol does not suppress renin by blocking muscarinic receptors.
Dopamine receptors in the proximal tubule do not account for the beta-blocker-associated decrease in renin.
key_expl: Juxtaglomerular cells express beta1 adrenergic receptors. Sympathetic beta1 stimulation promotes renin release, whereas beta1-selective blockers such as metoprolol decrease renin secretion in addition to their cardiac effects.
objective: Relate beta1 receptor blockade on juxtaglomerular cells to reduced renin release.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Glucocorticoids reduce neutrophil adhesion to endothelium and promote demargination from the vascular marginal pool, increasing circulating neutrophil counts despite suppression of inflammatory recruitment into tissues.
vignette: A 40-year-old woman receives high-dose prednisone for an autoimmune flare. The next day, her white blood cell count rises with neutrophil predominance, but she has no fever, new localizing symptoms, or hemodynamic instability.
lead: Which mechanism most directly explains the increase in circulating neutrophils?
correct: Reduced neutrophil adhesion to endothelium with demargination into the circulating pool
distractors: Increased neutrophil extravasation into inflamed tissues
Direct stimulation of bacterial colony growth in bone marrow
Enhanced eosinophil survival through interleukin-5 signaling
Increased expression of endothelial adhesion molecules
distractor_notes: Glucocorticoids reduce neutrophil migration into tissues rather than increasing it.
Corticosteroids do not raise neutrophils by stimulating bacterial growth in marrow.
Glucocorticoids generally reduce eosinophils and do not cause neutrophilia through IL-5-mediated eosinophil survival.
They reduce inflammatory adhesion signaling; increased endothelial adhesion would favor margination/extravasation rather than demargination.
key_expl: Glucocorticoids inhibit neutrophil adhesion to vascular endothelium and promote detachment from the marginal pool. This demargination increases the measured circulating neutrophil count even while tissue recruitment and inflammation are suppressed.
objective: Explain glucocorticoid-associated neutrophilia through neutrophil demargination.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Alpha1-mediated reversal of anaphylactic hypotension by epinephrine
mechanism: Epinephrine stimulates alpha1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction that raises systemic vascular resistance and helps reverse distributive hypotension and mucosal edema during anaphylaxis.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman develops diffuse urticaria, wheezing, and profound hypotension minutes after a bee sting. Intramuscular epinephrine is administered.
lead: Activation of which receptor most directly reverses the severe fall in systemic vascular resistance?
distractors: Beta1 adrenergic receptors
Beta2 adrenergic receptors
Muscarinic M3 receptors
Histamine H1 receptors
distractor_notes: Beta1 activation increases heart rate and contractility but does not most directly restore systemic vascular resistance.
Beta2 activation produces bronchodilation and some vascular smooth-muscle relaxation; it is not the principal receptor reversing distributive hypotension.
Muscarinic M3 activation does not mediate epinephrine's vasoconstrictor effect.
Histamine H1 activation contributes to allergic manifestations rather than reversing them.
key_expl: Epinephrine is first-line therapy for anaphylaxis because it addresses multiple life-threatening mechanisms. Its alpha1 effect causes systemic vasoconstriction, increasing vascular tone and blood pressure; beta2 stimulation separately improves bronchospasm.
objective: Identify alpha1 adrenergic vasoconstriction as the epinephrine effect that most directly reverses anaphylactic hypotension.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: IgE-mediated mast-cell activation in immediate hypersensitivity
mechanism: During sensitization, IgE binds high-affinity Fc epsilon RI receptors on mast cells. On re-exposure, multivalent allergen cross-links receptor-bound IgE, triggering mast-cell activation and rapid mediator release.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy with peanut allergy accidentally ingests a peanut-containing dessert and within minutes develops urticaria, bronchospasm, and facial swelling.
lead: Which event most directly triggers the immediate mast-cell response after re-exposure to the allergen?
correct: Cross-linking of Fc epsilon RI-bound IgE on mast cells
distractors: Binding of IgG to Fc gamma receptors on erythrocytes
Deposition of circulating immune complexes in small vessels
Activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognizing MHC class I
Cross-linking of IgM on naive B cells without mast-cell involvement
distractor_notes: IgG-mediated Fc receptor mechanisms are not the defining trigger of classic immediate type I hypersensitivity.
Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism.
Cytotoxic T-cell injury is a type IV hypersensitivity mechanism.
Naive B-cell IgM signaling does not directly trigger the rapid mast-cell degranulation of an established IgE-mediated allergy.
key_expl: Mast cells in sensitized patients carry allergen-specific IgE bound to high-affinity Fc epsilon RI. Re-exposure cross-links adjacent IgE-Fc epsilon RI complexes, initiating intracellular signaling and release of histamine and newly synthesized lipid mediators.
objective: Explain the immediate phase of type I hypersensitivity through allergen-mediated cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: C5a is a potent complement-derived neutrophil chemoattractant and anaphylatoxin generated during complement activation.
vignette: A patient with bacterial peritonitis has robust complement activation at the site of infection. Neutrophils are rapidly recruited from the bloodstream into the infected tissue.
lead: Which complement fragment most directly promotes this neutrophil chemotaxis?
distractors: C1q
C3b
C4b
C5b
distractor_notes: C1q initiates the classical complement pathway by recognizing immune complexes but is not the principal neutrophil chemoattractant.
C3b is a major opsonin that promotes phagocytosis; it is not the dominant complement chemotactic fragment.
C4b participates in classical/lectin pathway convertase formation and is not the major neutrophil chemoattractant.
C5b initiates assembly of the membrane attack complex rather than driving neutrophil chemotaxis.
key_expl: C5a is among the most potent complement-derived inflammatory mediators. It functions as an anaphylatoxin and strongly attracts and activates neutrophils, whereas C3b mainly opsonizes microbes and C5b initiates membrane attack complex formation.
objective: Identify C5a as the complement fragment responsible for potent neutrophil chemotaxis.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute bacterial meningitis typically produces elevated opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated CSF protein, and reduced CSF glucose relative to serum.
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and confusion. Lumbar puncture is performed after appropriate initial assessment.
lead: Which cerebrospinal fluid profile is most consistent with acute bacterial meningitis?
correct: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose
distractors: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein
Eosinophilic pleocytosis, low protein, and elevated glucose
Normal cell count, normal protein, and low opening pressure
Lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low protein, and elevated glucose
distractor_notes: This pattern is more typical of uncomplicated viral meningitis, in which CSF glucose is generally preserved.
Eosinophils with low protein and high glucose are not the classic bacterial meningitis profile.
Acute bacterial meningitis usually causes inflammatory CSF abnormalities and often elevated rather than low opening pressure.
Very low CSF protein and elevated glucose do not characterize bacterial meningitis.
key_expl: Bacterial invasion of the meninges produces a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory response, increased blood-CSF barrier permeability with elevated protein, and reduced CSF glucose. These findings contrast with the more commonly lymphocytic and glucose-preserved pattern of viral meningitis.
objective: Recognize the characteristic cerebrospinal fluid profile of acute bacterial meningitis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Rifampin-mediated reduction in oral contraceptive exposure
mechanism: Rifampin is a potent inducer of drug-metabolizing enzymes, particularly CYP3A4, and transport proteins such as P-glycoprotein, increasing clearance of many concurrently administered drugs including hormonal contraceptives.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive begins rifampin-containing therapy for active tuberculosis. Several weeks later, she develops breakthrough bleeding despite taking her contraceptive consistently.
lead: Which mechanism most likely explains the reduced contraceptive effectiveness?
correct: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4 with increased metabolism of contraceptive hormones
distractors: Inhibition of hepatic CYP3A4 with decreased hormone metabolism
Competitive blockade of estrogen receptors by rifampin
Suppression of intestinal bile acid synthesis preventing all steroid absorption
Irreversible inhibition of renal organic anion secretion
distractor_notes: Rifampin is a potent inducer rather than inhibitor of CYP3A4.
Rifampin does not reduce contraceptive efficacy by acting as an estrogen-receptor antagonist.
Its clinically important interaction is enzyme/transporter induction, not complete blockade of steroid absorption through bile-acid suppression.
Renal organic-anion transport inhibition is not the principal mechanism of the hormonal contraceptive interaction.
key_expl: Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4 and other drug-metabolizing pathways. Increased metabolism lowers exposure to estrogen and progestin components of oral contraceptives and can reduce contraceptive effectiveness.
objective: Explain rifampin-associated drug interactions through hepatic cytochrome P450 induction.
